sources.news_title: US, Canada fail to reach trade pact to avert Trump tariffs
sources.text:
Dominic LeBlanc, Canada’s minister in charge of US-Canada trade. Photo / Amid Farahi, AFP
Hefty US tariffs on some Canadian products have taken effect after days of negotiations that went down to the wire failed to produce an agreement.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed that his country will match the US tariffs “dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses”, after officialssaid that Washington and Ottawa had not managed to strike a deal.
The lack of a final agreement means that new 50% duties, set to impact some US$20 billion of Canadian exports to the United States, are now in effect.
Impacted products range from hockey sticks to cement.
US trade representative Jamieson Greer told reporters that “Canada declined to finalise the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week”.
That came despite Washington’s offers for tariff reductions in sectors like steel and aluminium, he added.
A senior US official said there are no further scheduled meetings for now.
The surprise announcement came after Trump said that the United States “should be able to have a deal with Canada,” citing his “good relationship” with Carney.
After many hours of trade talks last week, however, Canada’s top negotiator Dominic LeBlanc told reporters that officials still “have more work to do”.
LeBlanc and Greer also met for around three hours on Thursday.
Greer said that the Trump administration put on the table “significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminium, autos and lumber” in exchange for concessions from Canada.
He said that Canada was also maintaining its “prolonged retaliation” against the United States, including prohibitions on certain American goods and services.
Canada’s regional leaders said previously that the United States was particularly irritated by one retaliatory measure: the removal of US alcohol and wine from liquor stores.
But Carney said in a statement that “last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal”.
While Washington and Ottawa made “important progress” in recent weeks, Carney said, this “has not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians”.
The senior US official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Canada had sought additional concessions that the United States was unable to provide.
But they added that talks were candid and not acrimonious.
‘Significant pressure’ for US, Canada to de-escalate
Ryan Majerus, a former US commerce official, told AFP that “if Canada has agreed to also impose retaliatory tariffs, that will make de-escalating this a lot harder”.
“But I think both sides will face significant pressure in the coming days to find an off-ramp,” added Majerus, a trade lawyer with King & Spalding.
Christopher Padilla, another former US official who is now with Brunswick Group, told AFP there has been “a lot of hope among businesses on both sides” for a deal to “turn the page on what has been a very difficult 18 months in the US-Canada relationship”.
The White House had alleged “discriminatory treatment” by Canada against US alcohol, automobile and dairy products in introducing the duties.
They were originally set to take effect on Wednesday, before Trump issued a last-minute delay of three days, citing major progress in talks.
Canadian negotiators have been camped out in Washington to firm up a deal that aimed to address various flashpoints.
Canada has been seeking relief from Trump’s tariffs on autos, steel and aluminium, which have battered the country’s economy, forced job losses and strained what was once an iron-clad trade relationship.
Carney has repeatedly told Canadians that relations with the United States have been forever changed, regardless of what happens with an individual trade deal.
He says the country must diversify and reduce its reliance on the United States, which currently accounts for roughly 70% of Canadian exports.
Beyond the latest tariffs, the United States and Canada still have to agree on revisions to the North American free trade agreement, USMCA, which Trump declined to renew in its current form.

sources.news_title: Carney says Canada will match US tariffs 'dollar for dollar' after failed trade negotiations
sources.text:
Canada vows to match US tariffs 'dollar for dollar' after failed trade negotiations
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed that his country will match the US tariffs "dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses", after hefty US tariffs on some Canadian products took effect on Saturday following days of failed negotiations.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday he would slap retaliatory tariffs on the United States after walking away from a "bad deal" on trade, deepening the rift between the longtime allies.
Negotiations between the neighboring countries broke down on Friday in Washington, allowing new 50-percent US tariffs impacting some $20 billion worth of goods, or 5.5 percent of Canadian exports to the United States, to come into force.
Impacted products range from hockey sticks to cement.
US President Donald Trump had said Washington "should be able to have a deal with Canada," citing his "good relationship" with Carney.
But on Saturday, the Canadian prime minister said Trump had set conditions that were ultimately unacceptable.
"We believed earlier this week that we were moving towards a mutually beneficial agreement," Carney said in the Canadian capital Ottawa.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
"In recent days, the United States proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits for Canada, and called into question the reliability of any deal. In short, they asked too much and they offered too little," he said.
"We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked," Carney said, accusing Trump of launching a trade "war."
"You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," Carney said.
New Canadian tariffs will notably target the US steel and dairy industries, and take effect on September 8. Carney said further details would come next week.
On Friday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Washington had offered "significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber" in exchange for concessions from Canada.
A senior US official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, characterized the talks as candid and not acrimonious, but said there were no further scheduled meetings.
'Significant pressure'
Canada has been seeking relief from Trump's tariffs on autos, steel and aluminum, which have battered the country's economy, forced job losses and strained what was once an iron-clad trade relationship.
Canadian negotiators had been camped out in Washington this week to firm up a deal that aimed to address various flashpoints.
The White House had alleged "discriminatory treatment" by Canada against US alcohol, automobile and dairy products in introducing the duties.
They were originally set to take effect on Wednesday, before Trump issued a last-minute delay of three days, citing major progress in talks.
Ryan Majerus, a former US commerce official who now is a trade lawyer with King & Spalding, told AFP that "both sides will face significant pressure in the coming days to find an off-ramp."
Beyond the latest tariffs, the United States and Canada still have to agree on revisions to the North American free trade agreement, USMCA, which Trump declined to renew in its current form.
Bilateral ties also have been hurt by Trump's repeated threats to make Canada the 51st US state.
Trump was irked by Carney's widely-touted January speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland in which the prime minister declared that the global order was experiencing a "rupture."
Read moreTrump threatens 100% tariffs on Canadian goods over pending China trade deal
The Canadian leader has repeatedly said that relations with the United States have been forever changed, and that the country must reduce its reliance on the United States, which currently accounts for roughly 70 percent of Canadian exports.
"We've been under no illusions. We recognized from the start that America has changed," Carney told reporters on Saturday.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

sources.news_title: U.S. is set to impose 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian products
sources.text:
The United States imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian products early on Saturday (August 22, 2026), and Canada immediately said it would retaliate, after last-ditch negotiations failed to resolve the latest strain in already tense relations between the historic allies.
President Donald Trump’s import taxes will hit about 5% of what Canada ships to the United States every year, including products ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors.
“Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement. The retaliation escalates the trade conflict and calls into question the future of a North American trade pact between the United States, Canada and Mexico that is crucial to industry in all three countries.
Canada sought concessions on Trump tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber that the United States was unwilling to provide, a senior Trump administration official told reporters.
“Tonight, Canada declined to finalise the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week. Despite the US offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk-backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days,” U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement read to reporters on a press call shortly before midnight.
Mr. Carney blamed Washington for the breakdown, saying “last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.” He said he had suspended negotiations and directed Canada’s negotiating team to return to Ottawa.
Mr. Carney said his government would announce additional support for Canadian workers and businesses in the coming days.
Mr. Greer said the U.S. offer was “forward-looking” and included “a historic economic and national security partnership.” No further talks have been planned. The breakdown in negotiations marked a sharp reversal from two days earlier, when officials from the two countries sounded as if they were headed toward a compromise.
Mr. Carney said Canada’s goal throughout the negotiations had been to secure the best possible agreement, “never a deal at any price or on any deadline.”
A typically cooperative alliance goes sour
The political impact will likely be even bigger than the economic fallout. The countries sold each other $880 billion worth of goods and services last year.
The tariffs were initially supposed to kick in at 12:01 am Wednesday (August 19, 2026). But Mr. Trump extended the deadline for three days to allow talks to continue, but the two countries still could not reach an agreement in time.
The two countries have wrangled for decades over trade, poking each other over sore spots like Canadian softwood lumber imports and US access to Canada’s protected dairy market.
Somehow, they still managed to remain friends, allies and trading partners. Canadian soldiers fought alongside Americans in Afghanistan after 9/11. The 5,525-mile U.S.-Canada border is undefended, and nearly 330,000 people and $2 billion worth of goods cross it every day; 8,00,000 Canadians live in the United States.
Mr. Trump’s approach to dealing with Canada marks an extraordinary departure from the traditionally cooperative relationship between the two countries. Mr. Trump has hit Canadian goods with tariffs — in a push to bring manufacturing back to the United States — and has repeatedly made inflammatory comments about turning Canada into America’s 51st state.
Carney said Canada had recognised that “America has changed” and that the two countries would “not return to our old relationship.”
Canadians and Americans are frustrated
The Canadian public is fed up. A petition to expel the U.S. Ambassador, a Trump ally, has collected nearly 248,000 signatures since July 21. It accuses Ambassador Pete Hoekstra of having “normalised” Mr. Trump’s talk of annexing Canada, among other things.
The two countries had good reasons to find a compromise.
Nearly 72% of Canada’s goods exports last year went to the United States. And the Trump administration might be wary of imposing a hefty new tariff — paid by U.S. importers who try to pass along the cost to consumers via higher prices — ahead of November’s midterm elections. American voters are already frustrated with the high cost of living.
“Canada likely wanted further sector-specific relief than the U.S. was willing to offer, or Canada’s concessions did not go far enough,” said Ryan Majerus, a partner at King & Spalding and a former U.S. trade official. “Either way, I think both sides will be under immense pressure in the coming days to still find an off-ramp. But if Canada has agreed to also impose tariffs, the off-ramp may be even harder to find.” Candace Laing, president and CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, called the tariffs “a body blow to North American competitiveness,” warning they would raise costs for Americans while threatening Canadian customers, investment and small businesses.
Trump has turned to Depression-era tariffs
Mr. Trump has made tariffs the centrepiece of his second-term economic agenda. Last year, he imposed double-digit import taxes on almost every country, justifying them by declaring the longstanding U.S. trade deficit a national emergency. The Supreme Court in February ruled that he’d overstepped his authority, striking down those tariffs and setting the stage for the federal government to pay refunds to importers.
So Mr. Trump has looked for other legal authority to justify tariffs.
To hit Canada, he reached back to the Great Depression, invoking Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to threaten 50 per cent tariffs on products that account for about 5 per cent of Canadian exports to the United States.
Nearly a century ago, with the U.S. and world economies in collapse, Congress passed the 1930 tariff law, imposing taxes on imports from around the world. Known as the Smoot-Hawley tariffs after their congressional sponsors, they are notorious among economists and historians for limiting world commerce and making the Great Depression worse.
Section 338, which has never been used before to impose tariffs, authorises the President to slap import taxes of up to 50% on imports from countries that have discriminated against U.S. businesses. No investigation is required to justify the levies. Nor is there any limit on how long they can stay in place.
The rift comes as the United States, Mexico and Canada are trying to renew a trade agreement that Mr. Trump negotiated in his first term and once praised as a triumph. The United States has begun formal talks with Mexico over revamping the U.S-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). But talks with Canada have not begun, and escalating trade conflict casts doubt on whether they will.
“Canada told the Americans in advance that if these tariffs landed, it would stop negotiating and retaliate,” said Barry Appleton, senior fellow at the Centre for International Law at New York Law School. ”The American trade representative said publicly he would not tolerate retaliation. Both sides have now committed themselves in public, which is how escalation stops being a choice.”

sources.news_title: Canada suspends US trade talks over tariff dispute: PM
sources.text:
Canada has suspended trade negotiations with the United States, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Friday, citing insufficient progress in talks ahead of a deadline for new US tariffs.
Carney said Ottawa had worked to secure what he called a fair deal that would provide greater access to the US market and more certainty for Canadian businesses and workers.
“However, that progress has not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians,” Carney said in a statement.
“As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the US and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa,” he added.
Tariff dispute
Carney said Canadian negotiators had worked “hard, in good faith” to defend the country’s interests until the “very last minute”.
He said last-minute changes to the US-proposed terms were “unfair, uneconomic” and raised questions about the reliability of any potential deal.
Carney said the US intended to impose a 50 percent tariff on roughly $28 billion of Canadian goods at midnight.
“Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses,” he said.
Trade negotiations in Washington resumed on Friday morning ahead of the midnight deadline for the tariffs to take effect.
Both sides had previously said they were close to an agreement, with US President Donald Trump saying on Wednesday that a “very fair” deal had been reached.
Carney said Ottawa had made important progress towards securing what he described as the best possible deal with Washington, but that the remaining differences prevented Canada from meeting its objectives.

sources.news_title: PM Carney says Canada intends to match U.S. tariffs ‘dollar for dollar,’ after suspending trade negotiations
sources.text:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says U.S. President Donald Trump’s new 50 per cent tariffs amount to an economic “attack” on Canada. He has vowed “dollar for dollar” retaliatory tariffs on Sept. 8.
His remarks come after a late-night decision to call off trade talks with the U.S. He says last-minute requests from the American delegation led to a breakdown in negotiations, and that Canada is at economic “war” with the U.S.
Trump’s 50 per cent tariffs target US$20 billion worth of Canadian goods, including cement and hockey sticks.
Follow for key updates:
Canada ‘at war?’
Carney was asked: “Why does it feel like, today, Mark Carney is going to war, trade war?”
“You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” he responded.
He said Canada had waited for the U.S. to implement tariffs to respond this way, and now that they have, “we’ve got the reserves. We’ve got the resilience”
“We’ve got the plan, we’ve got the focus,” he continued. “We’re going to focus on what we can control. We’re going to build.”
Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist
PM: Retaliatory tariffs to come after Labour Day
Carney said retaliatory tariffs, in response to Trump’s new levies, will come into force on Sept. 8.
In his address on Saturday, Carney acknowledged that the tariffs will “raise costs and reduce choice” for Canadians.
But at the same time, we take this step confident that it is in the best interest of Canada, and that by rejecting a bad deal by standing up for Canada, (we focus) on what we can control,” he said.
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
U.S. proposals would turn Canada into 51st state: Eby
B.C. Premier David Eby says a request from U.S. negotiators would have effectively reduced Canada to America’s 51st state.
“The suggestion that Canada would not trade with other countries or reduce our trade with other countries because the Americans tell us to would reduce us to the economic equivalent of the 51st state,” said Eby, fresh from a meeting with Carney, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and other premiers.
Earlier today, Carney was asked for specifics on what he called new and “economically unfair” terms proposed by American negotiators.
He said the U.S. had made efforts to “restrict our ability to have other trade deals” in the last hours of trade talks.
“The prime minister and his team rightly walked away from any suggestion that we would agree to that,” said Eby.
Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist
Mark Carney chairs first ministers’ meeting
The Prime Minister’s Office says Mark Carney met virtually with provincial and territorial premiers Saturday to discuss the suspension of trade negotiations with the United States.
The PMO says Carney outlined next steps to protect Canadian interests, including dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs that will take effect on the Tuesday after Labour Day, along with additional measures to support Canadian workers and businesses affected by U.S. tariffs.
Carney also emphasized the importance of a united “Team Canada” approach, with continued collaboration between the federal, provincial and territorial governments on nation-building projects, diversifying export markets and removing internal trade barriers.
Tammy Ibrahimpour, CTV News National Digital Producer
Canada avoided a ‘chokehold’
International trade analyst and government affairs specialist at Gowling WLG Jacques Shore says by walking away from the tariff talks, Canada has avoided a “chokehold.”
In an interview with CTV News Channel, Shore described the situation as a “missed opportunity” for the United States.
He said the last-minute conditions put forward in the talks by the U.S. were “surprising.”
Shore highlighted that it would be hard to imagine that “we would be restricted from engaging with other countries” and making decisions that are only Canada’s to make.
He said despite these “trade tensions,” Canada and the U.S. are integrated and will be working together.
Shore added that, at this point, there are “Americans who are scratching their heads wondering how this could have happened to Canada.”He said this will “harm the American economy,” but Canada alsohas to brace itself.
Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist
F bombs in a trade war
California Governor Gavin Newsom made his feelings clear on social media Saturday morning.
“Our closest ally. Our critical trading partner. And Trump is hitting Canada with 50% tariffs,” wrote Newsom on X. “What the actual f--- are we doing?”
Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist
Deal would have not brought back auto jobs to Brampton: mayor
Patrick Brown, the mayor of Brampton, Ont., also commended the prime minister’s decision not to accept a bad deal and to match the new U.S. tariffs.
“This is not a trade war that we have asked for. Unfortunately, we’re in it because of the misguided policies of Donald Trump. But it doesn’t mean we should take it lying down,” Brown said in an interview with CP24 on Saturday afternoon.
“When I hear the premier and the prime minister say tariff for tariff, it’s our only recourse. We can’t continue to be bullied by this president.”
He noted that the reported terms of the deal that included permanent tariffs on the auto sector wouldn’t have brought the jobs at the Stellantis Brampton Assembly Plant, which has been idling since 2023.
Last week, Unifor claimed that Stellantis was seriously considering closing and selling the plant.
“Stellantis made it clear to me that as long as there are tariffs, there was no business case for auto production in Canada, and they were leaving until tariffs were lifted. So, I’m glad the prime minister didn’t accept a bad deal,” Brown said.
“It would not have salvaged the auto sector in Canada.”
Bryann Aguilar, CP24.com/CTVNews.ca journalist
‘Uncertainty better than certainty around a bad deal’
President and CEO of Global Automakers of Canada Lucas Malinowski believes it’s “unfortunate” that the U.S. and Canada couldn’t come to an agreement regarding the auto industry.
In an interview with CTV News Channel, he said the North American auto sector has incurred $110 billion in tariff-related costs over the past year and a half, making the industry “less competitive” and cars “more expensive” for consumers.
Yet, he admitted that, at the end of the day, “uncertainty is still better than certainty around a bad deal.”
Malinowski also said the deal on the table was “untenable,” based on Prime Minister Carney’s remarks and what the government has said.
Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist
‘Two-year root canal’ ahead for Canadians, Sarnia mayor says
Sarnia, Ont., Mayor Mike Bradley says Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision regarding the tariff talks was “100 per cent” correct but admits “the tough stuff” will now start.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration will “search and destroy” every relationship it has around the world in the next two years, including ties with Canada, he said in an interview with CTV News Channel. “Canadians need to stand together.”
Bradley said the situation for Canadians will be like a “permanent root canal for the next year or two,” but added that “it will be worth it.”
Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist
‘There are no deals’ with Trump: Former Harper aide
Former Director of Communications to Stephen Harper Kory Teneycke believes Prime Minister Mark Carney should prepare the nation for an “incredibly difficult period of time,” but supports Canada’s approach in the tariff talks.
In an interview with Vassy Kapelos on CTV News Channel, he said that if there is one thing we’ve learned from U.S. President Donald Trump, it’s that “there are no deals.”
Teneycke described Trump as a president who “has broken every agreement he has made on every topic” since he took office.
“He is the kind of guy who starts bombing you when you’re in peace talks,” he said, adding that Canada didn’t start this war, but “we’re going to be there to finish it.”
Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist
No deal was ‘surprising’: trade lawyer
Greg Kanargelidis, an international trade lawyer, said not reaching an agreement with the U.S. over the tariffs was “surprising”.
In an interview with CTV News Channel on Saturday, he said, “it was surprising to hear… about talks collapsing.”He said Canadian importers will be impacted by tariffs, but they could, in part, be compensated for through remissions orders.
The trade lawyer added that the tariffs will also impact a wide range of goods, including agricultural products, wood products, electronics, sporting goods, dairy and alcohol.
He noted the impact for companies in those industries will be “perhaps impossible to withstand.”.
Kanargelidis said the discussions could also serve as a “base” for CUSMA negotiations but admitted they may be at a “standstill” for the time being.
Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist
Trump ‘can’t be trusted’: Ford
Ontario Premier Doug Ford criticized U.S. President Donald Trump, portraying him as an untrustworthy bully whose tariff strategy harms both Canadians and Americans.
He says Trump “can’t be trusted” because “he changes the deal” and “keeps moving the goalpost.”
Speaking to reporters, Ford added that Trump is “the type of person that would steal your lunch money the first day, he’d steal the toque off your head the second day, and the third day he’d steal your running shoes.”
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
‘No deal is better than a bad deal’: Ford told Carney in letter
In a newly released letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney, Ontario Premier Doug Ford urged Ottawa to stand firm against the United States after President Donald Trump’s latest tariffs took effect following the collapse of last-minute trade talks.
The premier had largely remained quiet in recent days as negotiations continued.
However, in the letter, Ford told Carney that “no deal is better than a bad deal” that could encourage the United States to seek further concessions from Canada.
“We cannot allow arbitrary deadlines, shifting justifications or escalating tariff threats to weaken our resolve,” Ford wrote.
He said Ontario would not support removing its existing retaliatory measures without a deal that provides “significant relief” for Ontario workers, businesses and key sectors
Jermaine Wilson, CTVNews.ca Journalist
PM: U.S. proposed new ‘unfair’ terms
Carney said that progress was being made on negotiations towards a “mutually beneficial deal.” But in recent days, American negotiators proposed “new terms that were economically unfair.”
The terms “undermined net benefits for Canadians and called into question the reliability of any deal,” he said.
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
Last-minute changes
Carney was asked to specify what the U.S. sought to change in the final hours of negotiations.
Among those changes, he said the Americans had proposed a treatment of auto trade that was unacceptable to the Canadian team.
He also said the U.S. had taken “efforts to restrict our ability to have other trade deals,” and that “we believe in free trade.”
Carney was asked later if Canada had any of its own last-minute requests.
“’No’ is the short answer,” he responded.
Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist
Changes included auto, trade restrictions
The U.S. made “last-minute” requests to change the deal regarding the auto sector and Canada’s capacity to have other trade accords, according to Carney.
“The Americans wanted to limit it to autos only, not include medium and heavy duty trucks which is a big change, obviously,” he said.
Negotiators also introduced “at the last hour” efforts to restrict Canada’s ability to have other trade deals, he added.
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
Would Canada tariff other countries in co-ordination with U.S.?
When asked by a reporter if the U.S. expected Canada to tariff other countries as part of a trade deal, Carney responded, “there were elements of that.”
Canada could agree to that as part of an “integrated” market system with the U.S., Carney added.
But if that’s what the Americans are after, Carney said American tariffs on Canadian exports should be “clearly the lowest” among trading partners.
Asked why he thought the U.S. was interested in influencing Canadian foreign trade policy, Carney said “it’s a power play.”
Devika Desai and Luca Caruso-Moro,, CTVNews.ca journalist
B.C. Premier to address trade talks at 3 p.m. EDT
B.C. Premier David Eby will address the breakdown in trade talks in Vancouver at 3 p.m. EDT.
This follows the prime minister’s own remarks earlier today on the breakdown in negotiations between Canada and U.S. trade representatives shortly before the Trump’s tariff deadline expired.
In a social media post earlier today, Eby stated that “British Columbians will always stand with Canada.”
“We didn’t ask for this, but we’ll keep fighting for as long as it takes,” his post reads.
Follow along for more information here.
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
‘Mastering energy is mastering destiny’
Carney said Canada has been putting efforts towards ‘mastering energy’ and becoming an independent superpower.
“We’ve doubled the capacity of our electrical network from (now) to 2050,” he said.
He referred to an announcement made on Monday by federal government, Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador, to update and expand the Churchills Falls generating station, as well as develop the Gull island project and transmissions.
He described it as the “single largest investment in Canada’s history to build the largest clean energy project.”
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
PM: Canada investing local
Canada will invest $25 billion to protect workers and businesses affected by the tariffs, Carney said.
This will include investments in “equipment, productivity and supply chain resilience,” as well as financing large companies to keep employers “afloat,” he added.
“We’re helping those hardest hit industries retool and pivot to those new international markets, and we’re being our own best customers,” he said.
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
PM: Tariffs will hit U.S. steel and dairy
Carney said the retaliatory tariffs will hit sectors such as steel, dairy, appliances, agriculture, electronics.
“Also include products that are currently subject to unjustified Section 232 tariffs. This is a focused response to protect and defend our industries and allow them to compete with U.S. products in the Canadian market,” he said.
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
Premier pushback did not ‘factor’ in negotiations
Pushback from premiers in recent days over returning U.S. booze to stores did not factor into suspending trade negotiations, Carney said.
“The essence of (Wednesday’s meeting) was ... that we were on a path to a potential deal that would give Canadians ... the best deal in all our strategic sectors,” he said.
The price for that deal was “worth paying,” he added.
Last-minute changes by the Americans made the deal ‘uneconomic’, he added. “So we’re not asking the premiers to do anything.”
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
Tariff protection for Canadians on its way
Carney said that tariff protection will be provided to business affected by the U.S. tariffs.
“Many of them are small, medium-sized businesses,” he said. “They’re in a wide range of industries spread across the country, concentrated (in) Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia.”
He did not say when the protections will be announced but added that it will be released “in a few days.”
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
Trump tariffs ‘deeply troubling’: Business CEO
The CEO of a national business non-profit called the tariffs “deeply troubling” for thousands of small Canada businesses.
“A full 40 per cent of small exporters sell items on the new 10+ page list of items facing 50 per cent tariffs. Many CFIB members have said this will end their U.S. sales, and some have reported this will kill their businesses,” Dan Kelly, president and CEO of the Canadian Federation of Independent Businesses said.
“I hope that discussions continue and an interim deal can be quickly found.”
Read more here on how people are responding after the U.S. tariffs came into effect on Saturday.
Devika Desai CTVNews.ca journalist
Diversifying trade is ‘Plan A’
Carney said he will continue to focus on “building at home and diversifying trade abroad.”
“It has been our Plan A from the start,” he said.“Canada will continue to pursue this path to build Canada strong because it’s right and because it’s working,” he said.
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
Trouble in Steel City
Andrea Horwath, mayor of Hamilton, Ont., says the breakdown of tariff negotiations is extremely concerning.
She says Hamilton is a steel and manufacturing city with a large agricultural sector, and the uncertainty ahead will be stressful for many of its residents.
Horwath called on federal and provincial leaders to stand behind Canadian workers and industries.
Hamilton is responsible for approximately 60 per cent of Canada’s steel output.
The Canadian Press
Poilievre: Canada can’t accept one-way tariffs
“Canada cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialize our country. Nor can we accept a bad deal,” reads a statement from Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre Saturday morning.
He said his party is disappointed with the Americans’ move to impose new tariffs, calling them “unjustified” and adding they “threaten the jobs and livelihoods of families right across our country.”
He also called on the Liberal government to end its industrial carbon levy and enact “major tax reforms” to spur investment, among other measures.
Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca Journalist
Premiers respond to failed trade talks
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the “prime minister has my full support for a strong response—tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar.”
B.C. Premier David Eby, who was advocating for relief on softwood lumber tariffs, said Canada’s “politeness should never be mistaken for weakness.”
There is frustration, however, from Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who says she is “deeply disappointed” that no deal was reached and is “urging the federal government to restart negotiations as soon as possible.”
Stephanie Ha, CTV News’ Ottawa News Bureau manager. Read the full story here.
Here is everything that happened on Aug. 21:
PM Carney says Canada intends to match the U.S. tariffs ‘dollar for dollar’
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s office released a statement ahead of the deadline saying he suspended trade negotiations with the United States, setting in motion the 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods.
“I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa. They have worked hard, in good faith, to defend the interests of Canadians throughout these negotiations up until the very last minute,” the PMO said in the statement.
“However, last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”
“At midnight tonight, the U.S. intends to impose a 50% tariff on roughly $28 billion of Canadian goods,” the statement read.
“Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses.”
Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca Journalist
Canada has declined to finalize the trade deal, ‘upended’ balance: Greer
In a statement released Friday night, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Canada has declined to finalize the deal and “upended” the balance reached during the negotiations.
“Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walkbacks of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days,” the statement said.
“In addition, Canada is continuing to maintain its prolonged retaliation against the United States, including, among other things, flat-out prohibitions on certain American goods and services.”
The statement went on to say that Canada declined the deal despite the U.S. offering Canada “better treatment” and “significant tariff reductions” on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber in exchange for concessions.
“The U.S. offer was also forward-looking and included a historic economic and national security partnership to cooperate on export controls, combat transshipment, enhance digital trade, and align certain external tariffs,” Greer said in the statement.
“This is a missed opportunity for Canada to partner with the United States, which is the fastest-growing economy in the G7.”
Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca Journalist
‘Tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar’: Ford extends support for prime minister
Ontario Premier Doug Ford extended his support for Prime Minister Mark Carney in a social media post, after the trade negotiations were suspended Friday night.
“Team Canada needs to stand together more united than ever before,” Ford said.
“The prime minister has my full support for a strong response—tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar. As we fight to protect Canadian sovereignty and economic security, everything needs to be on the table. Ontario is ready to do its part.”
Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca Journalist
‘We’ll keep fighting’: Eby
B.C. Premier David Eby, who was advocating for relief on softwood lumber tariffs, also responded to the news, saying Canada’s “politeness should never be mistaken for weakness.”
“We didn’t ask for this, but we’ll keep fighting for as long as it takes,” Eby added.
Stephanie Ha, CTV News’ Ottawa News Bureau manager
As tariff deadline approaches, dynamic ‘not going well:’ sources
With less than two hours until new 50 per cent tariffs are set to be imposed on a variety of Canadian goods, two sources close to the negotiations tell CTV News that there are some challenges with the dynamic in negotiations, particularly with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick who is involved in the final hours of talks.
According to the sources, the talks are focused on “just a couple” of outstanding issues, but some of the personal dynamics with Lutnick, who appears to have lingering feelings over recent issues with the Gordie Howe International Bridge, is a challenge. The opening of the bridge was delayed for weeks because of U.S. complaints over toll governance and revenue sharing, after which Canada agreed to share revenues earlier than planned.
Canada’s chief trade negotiator Janice Charette remains at the United States Representative’s office in Washington as of late Friday night as talks continue.
Stephanie Ha, CTV News’ Ottawa News Bureau manager
With files from CTV’s Chief Political Correspondent Vassy Kapelos and CTV’s Senior Political Correspondent Mike Le Couteur
‘Working up until the last minute’: LeBlanc
“We have more work to do,” LeBlanc told reporters as he exited the U.S. trade representatives office around 7:30 p.m. on Friday.
“We’re going to continue working up until the last minute. Our job is not finished. Canadian workers, Canadian businesses expect us to do all of this important work” he said.
Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist
‘I only make good deals,’ Trump says
“I only make good deals,” Trump told reporters on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
He was asked about progress toward a deal with Canada. He said talks were “moving along,” and that his team has a “good relationship” with Carney.
He didn’t offer details on the prospective deal.
“We have to take care of our farmers.”
Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist
A ‘low-key horrible’ deal: trade policy expert
Some concern about the deal still persists, an international trade policy researcher told CTV News Channel.
“For some of the leaks we’ve seen, it doesn’t sound like it’s going to be a good deal,” Stuart Trew said hours before the deadline on Friday.
“In fact, as my niece might say, it sounds ‘pretty low-key horrible’” Trew said, referring to tariffs that will remain on steel exports to the U.S.
“Aluminum (and) the auto tariffs, at least according to the leaks, being at 15 per cent would be – in the short-to-medium term – pretty unsustainable for the industry.”
Trew said such a deal would inevitably “eat into the reason to make any vehicles in Canada whatsoever.”
He cautioned against putting Canada in a worse position than before the trade war started by accepting a deal that would put U.S. booze back on the shelves and letting go of our retaliatory tariffs.
“The legitimate question is why would we come to such a bad deal now, when all we’re getting out of this is some kind of barely noticeable reprieve, right?”
Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist
‘Aiming to get the best agreement’: Alberta’s Smith
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is optimistic for a new trade deal with the United States, telling CTV News Calgary the best deal for Canada would involve no additional tariffs.
“I know everybody hopes that we could get 100 per cent of all products going across the border tariff free,” Smith said in an interview.
“But I think where we’re at in the negotiations is that we’re aiming to get the best agreement in the world of any nation with the United States and a reduction in the current tariffs that we have.”
It’s the first time Smith has spoken on the intense negotiations between Ottawa and Washington during trade deadline week.
Cassidy McMackon, CTV News Calgary, Digital Producer
Compromise a ‘hallmark’ of any good deal: former U.S. ambassador to Canada
For any good deal, there need to be concessions on both sides, according to former U.S. ambassador to Canada David L. Cohen.
Cohen told CTV News Channel Friday night that he has been “optimistic,” throughout the process and that although it might take both, Canada and the U.S. some time to reach an agreement, there will ultimately be one.
However, he said the “hallmark” of a good deal is when there is “some unhappiness” on both sides.
“There’s a compromise here, and it’s a compromise where Canada is giving something up, but the U.S. is giving something up too,” Cohen said.
“Both sides giving something up, both sides being a little unhappy with the landing place, but both sides looking at the bigger picture and understanding that there are huge benefits to both Canada and the U.S. to a resolution of this dispute, which has not benefited either country.”
Aarjavee Raaj, CTVNews.ca Journalist
Trade deal is an ‘economic security negotiation’: analyst
Following Trump’s comment that trade talks are moving along, an international trade analyst says securing a deal is now effectively an “economic security negotiation.”
“I feel for the number of companies, the factories, and all those that are engaged in looking at this carefully to ensure that they can continue to do business,” Jacques Shore told CTV News Channel on Friday.
Canada needs to reach a trade agreement “right now,” to ensure goods currently protected under CUSMA with no tariffs on them “remain as they are without this potential of 50 per cent,” Shore added.
Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist
Trump’s tariffs on autos ‘outrageous’: spokesperson
National spokesperson of the Canadian Automobile Dealers Association, Huw Williams believes that Canada and the U.S. should have completely automotive free trade as in the past 60 years but that must be viewed with a “dose of realism” that the other side is an unpredictable and “bombastic” administration.
“If the automotive industry remains competitive within the North American context, consumers will be the winner on both sides of the border,” he told CTV News Channel.
Williams described U.S. President Trump’s 25 per cent tariffs on autos as “outrageous” which he said is bad for consumers and dealers, both in the U.S and Canada.
Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca Journalist
Canadian importers need U.S. alcohol: executive
Stacy Kyle, executive director of the Import Vintners and Spirits Association, says she’s hoping premiers get American liquor back on store shelves, since is something she’s been asking for since the ban was put in place in March 2025.
“The importers are Canadian. They’re locals...and they’ve been impacted by this ban and unable to do business,” Kyle told CTV News Channel on Friday.
“So, it’s important for our members to have viable businesses and operations to maintain their relationships they’ve built with their suppliers.”
Elianna Lev, CTVNews.ca Journalist
We want to hear from you
Are you worried about how tariffs might affect your work? Have trade disruptions already impacted your job?
Share your story by emailing us at dotcom@bellmedia.ca with your name, general location and phone number in case we want to follow up.
Your comments may be used in a CTV News story.
Lumber industry needs certainty: expert
Executive director of the Independent Wood Processors Association of B.C. says that while he’s pleased softwood lumber has remained on the negotiating table, the industry needs certainty.
“Let’s keep in mind we’ve been at this for nine years. We had a tariff that started around eight per cent, now it’s up to 45 per cent and it could expand to 50 per cent,” Brian Menzies told CTV News Channel on Friday.
“I don’t think the outcome is going to be great, but at least there’ll be some certainty, and that’s what I want right now for our small businesses,” he said.
Menzies said about $11 billion in tariff deposits is currently being held at the border, and many small businesses have taken on significant financial risk, including using their homes as collateral to cover the required bonds.
“They want to see some resolution to this. They want to see some of those deposits returned to them as well because they have been paying it out of their own pocket to survive right now.”
Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist
Canadian team takes ‘working lunch’: source
A source from the Canadian team tells CTV News LeBlanc, Charette, Blanchard and Wiseman are participating in a “working lunch.”
Mike Le Couteur, Senior Political Correspondent
LeBlanc returns
LeBlanc just passed news cameras on his way back into the U.S. Trade Representative’s office for the first time since departing for lunch at around 1:20 p.m. ET – more than two hours ago.
He did not stop to speak to media.
Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist
‘It’s tricky for Mark Carney’: Former Alberta premier
Jason Kenney, the former premier of Alberta, says while trade talks appear to be going “in a pretty good direction,” he has concerns.
“I just hope that our government hasn’t made all sorts of preliminary concessions, and I say preliminary because this is an appetizer for the main meal, which is the CUSMA negotiation or renewal,” he told CTV News Channel on Friday.
Although Carney is well-equipped to handle negotiations, he is ultimately in a tough position explains Kenney.
“It’s tricky for Mark Carney. It couldn’t be trickier,” he said.
Kenney said the prime minister is likely torn between his commitment to aggressively defend the interests of Canadians’ in sectors including auto, while also creating “a space of some stability, knowing full well that based on past actions, the Trump administration could just do a 180 all over again.”
Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist
LeBlanc has entered the building
LeBlanc has entered the U.S. Trade Representatives office. He did not stop to take questions from reporters.
Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist
Negotiations may be ‘phased’
With hours left to deadline, a trade lawyer says Canadian and U.S. representatives may extended negotiations through the weekend and opt for a “phased approach.”
“There is going to be a good amount of negotiation left,” Robert Glasgow, international trade lawyer, told CTV News Channel on Friday.
“I think they’re almost certainly going to start segmenting it down ... but that’s probably going to take a few more days to negotiate,” he added.
The deal won’t eliminate tariffs entirely, Glasgow said, and Carney’s team is likely focused on preserving the CUSMA exemption and “drive tariffs as low as he can on as broad of a basis as he can get it.”
Under the CUSMA exemption, goods that comply with CUSMA rules of origin are generally exempt from U.S. blanket or general emergency tariffs.
While Carney has partially pivoted defence procurement to some European contractors, he will want to service “that segment with multinational and transnational participation of Canadian firms.”
“If we can focus on procuring from American companies that are producing domestically, we still retain that ... procurement base, while still potentially placating the demands of the American administration,” Glasgow said.
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
Trade talks today
This morning’s meeting between Canadian and American negotiators is expected to take place at 11:30 a.m., according to a source close to the talks.
Canada-U.S. Trade Minister LeBlanc, Chief Trade Negotiator Janice Charette and Carney’s Chief of Staff Marc-Andre Blanchard, are expected to attend.
Mike Le Couteur, Senior Political Correspondent and Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist
Deadline could be extended: political analyst
A former Trudeau staff member says that while a deal is hopefully signed tonight, she would not be surprised if the tariff deadline was extended again.
“We’re seeing a level of diffusion come out,” Sharan Kaur, former deputy chief of staff to former finance minister Bill Morneau, told CTV News Channel on Friday.
The U.S. president, the now-CTV News political analyst added, is known for making “flippant comments” when things aren’t going his way.
She also pointed to issues discussed this week like returning U.S. alcohol to Canadian stores. “These concessions ... are leverage,” she said. “... We have to get used to the fact that tariffs are going to be around in one way, shape or form. This is actually a positive discussion taking place.”
Canadians aren’t the only ones impacted; Trump also needs the deal, Kaur said.
“The whole anti-everything American sentiment ... is impacting them,” she said. “...Let’s also keep in mind that he’s got midterms coming up.”
It’s difficult to say if the deal could be trusted, she said. “He is known to rip deals, left, right and centre.”
“The goal is to ensure that the temperature is brought down and that they get to a point where industry is not suffering.”
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
This won’t be an ‘early night’
An international trade lawyer says he’s anticipating being up all night as he awaits final details from the Canadian government.
“Let’s put this way: I don’t think I’m going to have an early night,” Barry Appleton told CTV News on Friday. “But here’s the good part: they’re walking in the room. They’re still going to have more talks.”
Appleton said that the problem with the trade deal after Trump’s three-day reprieve is that it will likely leave numerous items unresolved.
“This is just a deal to get us talking again to have more of a deal, and what are we going to give up to have that? Right, that’s the question that we all want to know. And there’s so many different ideas circulating. That’s the part we got to figure out,” he said.
Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist
Poilievre to Carney: ‘Don’t take a bad deal’
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre repeated his call Friday for Prime Minister Mark Carney not to “take a bad deal.”
“Mr. Carney promised in the last election that he would be elbows up. He promised that he would negotiate a win,” Poilievre said in a press conference in Kitchener, Ont. on Friday. “In his words, he promised, and I quote, that he could ‘handle Trump.’ He promised he would not accept a bad deal. Mr. Carney, keep your promise. Fight for Canada.”
Asked by reporters if it’s acceptable for Canada to agree to a reduced tariffs on steel and aluminum, Poilievre said “no, absolutely not.”
“One-sided tariffs on Canadian industry would be a bad deal,” he added.
Stephanie Ha, CTV News’ Ottawa News Bureau manager
Booze ban ‘had its time’: Raitt
The decision to reverse provincial bans on U.S. alcohol may be the reason Canada secures a deal tonight, says Lisa Raitt, member of the Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations and former deputy leader of the Conservative Party of Canada.
She said Trump has made it very clear that he views the removal of American alcohol from Canadian store shelves as a discriminatory measure, and as a result, threatened 50 per cent tariffs on vulnerable industries.
“You have to do whatever you can to ensure that that didn’t happen, and that doesn’t happen tonight,” said Raitt.
“Asking the premiers to reverse their booze bans, I do believe, is an important part of the entire deal.”
She says while the alcohol ban was effective in getting U.S. attention, “it had its time.”
“The reality is that the leverage on this negotiation going around really did come from the U.S.,” says Raitt.
She says tariff pressure forced the two countries into important negotiations that have likely yielded results and “hopefully a deal that both sides can live with and can prosper with going forward.”
Anam Khan, BNN Bloomberg journalist
The ‘best deal’ for autos
Canada is in a position to get “the best deal” for its auto industry compared to the rest of the world, according to an industry representative.
Huw Williams, spokesperson for the Canadian Automobile Dealers Association, told CTV News Channel on Thursday that there is opportunity to get “a good short term deal that hopefully rolls into the CUSMA negotiations in the future.”
Canada is the biggest customer of U.S.-made vehicles, he said. “It doesn’t do well to attack your customer.”
Williams said they have asked their U.S. counterparts to communicate that the tariffs hurt the economy on both sides.
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
TSX shows gains
The S&P/TSX composite was up nearly a point (36,694, up 0.88 per cent) in Friday morning trading.
Energy and mining stocks showed the largest gains.
Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist
Anand talks Arctic, NATO with Rubio
While Canadian and U.S. negotiators hammer out the details of a deal, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand met with her American counterpart, Marco Rubio, for security talks today.
A readout from Anand’s office reports the two discussed “transnational fraudulent activity including scam centres,” Arctic foreign policy and NATO investments.
“Minister Anand highlighted that Canada will continue to engage constructively with the United States on trade and to strengthen our economic relationship,” the statement added.
Canada recently committed to spend five per cent of its GDP on defence by 2035. U.S. President Donald Trump has long pushed allied countries to increase their military investments.
Anand and Rubio will speak again in September at the United Nations.
Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist
PM tried to ‘out-tough’ Trump: Vance
U.S. Vice-President JD Vance said Carney tried to “out-tough” Trump in trade negotiations and credited Conservative MP Jamil Jivani as an “effective advocate” in the deal talks.
In audio from a Wednesday fundraiser in Southampton, N.Y., which was provided to The Canadian Press by a source who attended the private function, Vance said Carney is a “very sweet guy” and he gets along with him quite well.
But Carney “comes in and puffs his chest out and says, ‘I’m going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump,’” he added.
“It’s hilarious because Carney presents this as some victory for Canada when fundamentally, like, they climb down on a lot of issues,” Vance told the room.
“But the quiet sort of behind-the-scenes story is that this, like, random MP who has a good relationship with us has been a pretty effective advocate,” he said about Jivani.
Vance added there’s “this guy Pierre Poilievre, who is the leader of the Conservatives in Canada,” adding he is a “non-entity” in negotiations.
The White House and the vice-president’s office have not yet responded to a request for comment.
The Canadian Press. Read the full story here.
Vance’s comments are ‘childish,’ says ex-ambassador
Vance’s comments about Carney were “childish” and “flippant,” according to Gordon D. Giffen, who served as U.S. Ambassador to Canada from 1997 to 2001.
“The vice-president was out of line,” he told CTV News Channel from Brevard, N.C.
Asked what Canada should do next if a deal isn’t reached, Giffen said he doesn’t think the U.S. will follow through with imposing the 50 per cent tariffs as the president promised.
He called the new, 50 per cent tariffs “unsound, bad policy,” and predicted their imposition would beget further Canadian retaliation.
Luca Caruso-Moro, CTVNews.ca journalist
Winery owner unconcerned about U.S. booze return
An Ontario winery owner says he isn’t worried about a drop in sales should U.S. booze return to store shelves.
Donald Ziraldo, who is the founding chairman of the Vintners Quality Alliance (VQA), told CTV Your Morning on Friday that provincial bans have boosted sales at local wineries by 25 per cent to 100 per cent.
“People became more aware ... that the Niagara Canadian wines, in particular, are as good as the California, and probably a little bit less expensive,” he said.
Prime Minister Mark Carney asked premiers this week to lift their respective bans, which have been in place since February 2025. All have said they will comply.
The VQA is Canada’s Canada’s official regulatory and appellation of origin system for high-quality wines. A VQA label guarantees that a wine is made entirely from locally grown grapes in Ontario or B.C. and meets strict production and labeling standards.
Ziraldo added that he hopes Quebec and the Maritime provinces will join the alliance to let consumers know which wines are “100 per cent grown in Canada.”
Devika Desai, CTVNews.ca journalist
Sustainable profit margin a good deal for auto makers
Flavio Volpe, the president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers Association, said a good deal for his members is one that allows auto makers to have a sustainable profit margin.
“I think a lot of people who aren’t as familiar with the industry say, ‘Hey, look, if you go down from 25 to 15 (per cent tariffs), that sounds great,’” he told CTV News Channel on Friday.
However Volpe elaborated that even if U.S. tariffs on Canadian autos fall from 25 per cent to 15 per cent, that may not be enough to protect Canadian carmakers especially after being targeted “by Donald Trump’s White House and also our other main competitors, China, at the same time.”
Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist
LeBlanc on trade deal: ‘We’re very close’
Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc shared an update following a more than three-hour meeting with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Washington on Thursday, saying they are “very close” to an agreement.
“We continue to make progress, and we’re going to stay here and do the work that’s necessary until we get to that point,” LeBlanc said to reporters, while also describing the meeting as “long” and “detailed.”
Chief Trade Negotiator Janice Charette, Canadian Ambassador to the U.S. Mark Wiseman and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Chief of Staff Marc-André Blanchard were also involved in the meeting.
Stephanie Ha, bureau manager, Ottawa News Bureau
All provinces agreed to restock U.S. liquor: N.L. premier
Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham says Canada’s premiers have agreed to return U.S. alcohol to store shelves as part of the tentative trade deal with the U.S.
He said the prime minister is confident an agreement will be reached and that “as part of this agreement, he asked all of the provinces, as a sign of good faith, ‘would we put U.S. liquor back on our shelves,’ and we all agreed.”
Several of the premiers have not commented publicly on the issue.
U.S. alcohol products remain off the shelves in every province except Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Tiffany Hendsbee, CTV News supervising multiplatform writer

sources.news_title: U.S.-Canada trade talks collapse, massive tariffs to take effect
New tariffs take effect after trade talks between US, Canada fall apart
sources.text:
MADISON (WKOW) -- New 50% tariffs on some Canadian goods went into effect just after 11 p.m. central time Friday night, after the US and Canada failed to reach a trade deal.
ABC News reports the tariffs target dozens of products, including hockey sticks, whey protein and alcoholic beverages like wine and vodka. Both countries blamed the other for talks falling apart.
"Tonight, Canada declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week," the Office of the United States Trade Representative said in a post on X. "Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days. In addition, Canada is continuing to maintain its prolonged retaliation against the United States, including, among other things, flat-out prohibitions on certain American goods and services."
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also released a written statement on social media, saying he decided to suspend negotiations.
"Last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," Carney said.
He vowed to respond to the new American import taxes, promising to "match those tariffs dollar for dollar".
These new tariffs could have an impact on people and businesses in Wisconsin because Canada was the Badger State's largest export and import market in 2025, according to data from the International Trade Administration. Last year, Wisconsin exported $7.6 billion worth of goods to Canada and imported $5.7 billion worth of goods. Top import sectors included machinery, chemicals and computer & electronic products.

sources.news_title: US slaps 50% tariffs on US$20 billion of Canadian goods after trade talks fail
sources.text:
US slaps 50% tariffs on US$20 billion of Canadian goods after trade talks fail
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed retaliation and support measures, rejecting ‘unfair’ US demands as last-minute brinkmanship
The United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on US$20 billion worth of Canadian products early on Saturday and Canada immediately said it would retaliate, after last-ditch negotiations failed to resolve the latest strain in already tense relations between the historic allies.
US President Donald Trump’s import taxes will hit about 5 per cent of what Canada ships to the United States every year, including products ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors.
“Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement. The retaliation escalates the trade conflict and calls into question the future of a North American trade pact between the US, Canada and Mexico that is crucial to industry in all three countries.
Canada sought concessions on Trump tariffs on steel, aluminium, vehicles and timber that the US was unwilling to provide, a senior Trump administration official told reporters.
“Tonight, Canada declined to finalise the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week. Despite the US offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk-backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days,” US trade representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement read to reporters on a press call shortly before midnight.

sources.news_title: US-Canada trade talks fail, high tariffs kick in
sources.text:
WASHINGTON - Hefty US tariffs on some Canadian products took effect on Saturday after days of negotiations that went down to the wire failed to produce an agreement.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed that his country would match the US tariffs “dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses”, after officials said late Friday that Washington and Ottawa had not managed to strike a deal.
The lack of a final agreement means that new 50% duties, set to impact about $20 billion worth of Canadian exports to the United States, took effect on Saturday.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters on Friday that “tonight, Canada declined to finalise the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week”.
That came despite Washington’s offers for tariff reductions in sectors like steel and aluminum, he added.
The surprise announcement came after Trump said that the United States “should be able to have a deal with Canada”, citing his “good relationship” with Carney.
After hours of trade talks on Friday, however, Canada’s top negotiator Dominic LeBlanc told reporters that officials still “have more work to do.”
LeBlanc and Greer also met for around three hours on Thursday.
Greer said that the Trump administration put on the table “significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminium, autos and lumber” in exchange for concessions from Canada.
He said that Canada was also maintaining its “prolonged retaliation” against the United States.
But Carney said in a statement that “last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic and called into question the reliability of any deal.”
‘Discriminatory treatment’
Canada’s regional leaders said previously that the United States was particularly irritated by one retaliatory measure: the removal of US alcohol and wine from liquor stores.
The White House had alleged “discriminatory treatment” by Canada against US alcohol, automobile and dairy products in introducing the duties.
They were originally set to take effect on Wednesday, before Trump issued a last-minute delay of three days — citing major progress in talks.
Canadian negotiators have been camped out in Washington this week to firm up a deal that aimed to address various flash points.
Canada has been seeking relief from Trump’s tariffs on autos, steel and aluminum, which have battered the country’s economy, forced job losses and strained what was once an iron-clad trade relationship.
Carney has repeatedly told Canadians that relations with the United States have been forever changed, regardless of what happens with an individual trade deal.
He says the country must diversify and reduce its reliance on the United States, which currently accounts for roughly 70% of Canadian exports.
Beyond the ongoing negotiations, the United States and Canada still have to agree on revisions to the North American free trade agreement, USMCA, which Trump declined to renew last month.

Canada vows dollar-to-dollar tariff retaliation, suspends trade talks with U.S.
US-Canada trade war escalates as Trump imposes 50% tariffs
sources.text:
The United States imposed 50% tariffs on some $20 billion worth of Canadian products early Saturday, prompting an immediate pledge of retaliation from Ottawa after last-minute negotiations failed to resolve the latest crisis between the longtime allies.
The new import taxes affect roughly 5% of Canada’s annual exports to the United States and cover products ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada would match the U.S. tariffs dollar for dollar, escalating a trade confrontation that is increasingly raising questions about the future of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, the trade pact underpinning much of North American commerce.
Canada had sought relief from existing U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum, automobiles and lumber, but Washington was unwilling to grant the concessions Ottawa wanted. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer blamed Canada for the collapse of negotiations, saying Ottawa introduced new demands and reversed previous commitments shortly before the deadline.
“Tonight, Canada declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week,” Greer said in a statement read to reporters shortly before midnight. “Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk-backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days.”
Carney rejected that account, saying the terms had shifted at the last minute. “Last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal,” he said, adding that his government would announce further support for Canadian workers and businesses in the coming days.
Greer said the U.S. proposal had been “forward-looking” and offered what he described as “a historic economic and national security partnership.” No further negotiations have been scheduled. The breakdown represented a sharp reversal from just two days earlier, when officials from both countries had suggested a compromise was within reach.
Longtime allies enter a new phase of confrontation
The economic consequences could be significant, but the political fallout may prove even deeper. The United States and Canada traded roughly $880 billion in goods and services last year, and the two countries have long maintained one of the world’s closest economic and security relationships.
The tariffs had initially been scheduled to take effect Wednesday, but President Donald Trump extended the deadline by three days to allow negotiations to continue. Despite that reprieve, the two sides failed to bridge their differences.
Washington and Ottawa have clashed repeatedly over trade issues for decades, particularly Canadian softwood lumber and U.S. access to Canada’s protected dairy market. Those disputes, however, rarely threatened the broader alliance. Canadian troops fought alongside U.S. forces in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks, while the two countries share a 5,525-mile border crossed each day by hundreds of thousands of people and billions of dollars in trade.
Trump’s approach has sharply departed from that traditionally cooperative relationship. As part of his broader effort to shift manufacturing back to the United States, he has repeatedly imposed tariffs on Canadian goods and has also angered Canadians by suggesting that the country could become the 51st U.S. state.
Public frustration in Canada has grown accordingly. A petition seeking the expulsion of U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra, a Trump ally, has collected nearly 248,000 signatures since July 21. Its organizers accuse him, among other things, of helping normalize Trump’s rhetoric about annexing Canada.
Pressure grows for a way out
Both countries nevertheless have powerful incentives to avoid a prolonged trade war. Nearly 72% of Canadian goods exports went to the United States last year, making the U.S. market critical to the Canadian economy. For Washington, new tariffs could also prove politically costly because they are paid by U.S. importers, who can pass the added expense on to consumers already frustrated by the cost of living ahead of November’s midterm elections.
“Canada likely wanted further sector-specific relief than the U.S. was willing to offer, or Canada’s concessions did not go far enough,” said Ryan Majerus, a partner at King & Spalding and former U.S. trade official. “Either way, I think both sides will be under immense pressure in the coming days to still find an off-ramp. But if Canada has agreed to also impose tariffs, the off-ramp may be even harder to find.”
Candace Laing, president and CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, called the new tariffs “a body blow to North American competitiveness,” warning that they would raise costs for Americans while threatening Canadian customers, investment and small businesses.
The dispute is also unfolding as Washington, Ottawa and Mexico prepare for negotiations over the future of the USMCA, the agreement Trump negotiated during his first term and once hailed as a major achievement. The United States has already begun formal talks with Mexico on revising the pact, but negotiations with Canada have yet to begin.
Barry Appleton, senior fellow at the Center for International Law at New York Law School, said both sides had now made public commitments that would make de-escalation more difficult.
“Canada told the Americans in advance that if these tariffs landed, it would stop negotiating and retaliate,” he said. “The American trade representative said publicly he would not tolerate retaliation. Both sides have now committed themselves in public, which is how escalation stops being a choice.”

sources.news_title: U.S. to Impose 50% Tariffs on Canada After Talks Fail as Ottawa Plans Matching Duties
sources.text:
The U.S. was poised to move ahead early Saturday with 50% tariffs on $20 billion in Canadian goods after eleventh-hour negotiations failed to defuse the latest dispute between the longtime allies. Canada’s leader responded by vowing to match the duties “dollar for dollar.”
Speaking to reporters late Friday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Canada had refused to finalize a trade agreement on terms that he said had been settled earlier in the week.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, in a separate statement, said the “progress” made during the talks had “not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians.”
“As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa,” Carney said, adding that “Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses.”
President Trump’s new import taxes would apply to roughly 5% of Canada’s annual exports to the United States, covering items that range from hockey sticks to tongue depressors.
The economic damage may be limited compared with the broader political fallout. Canada has already warned it will answer any new U.S. tariffs with duties of its own, escalating a trade conflict between two countries that exchanged $880 billion in goods and services last year.
The tariffs had originally been scheduled to take effect at 12:01 a.m. Wednesday. Mr. Trump pushed the deadline back by three days to give negotiators more time, but the two sides were still unable to reach a deal before the extension expired.
Earlier in the week, Carney had said that “substantial progress has been made, although there is important work still to be done.”
The Trump administration currently imposes a 10% tariff on goods from Canada, the U.S.’s second-largest trading partner after Mexico, though most Canadian imports are exempt because they comply with the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a trade deal signed during Mr. Trump’s first term.
Mr. Trump has had a tense relationship with Canada due to trade, NATO, a dispute over a Detroit-area bridge and his threats to make Canada the U.S.’ 51st state.

sources.text:
US-Canada trade talks collapse, triggering 50% Trump tariffs
WASHINGTON – The US imposed 50 per cent tariffs on some Canadian goods on Aug 22 after the two longstanding allies failed to reach a trade deal, with each side accusing the other of derailing days of talks.
The tariffs that came into effect just after midnight (noon, Singapore time) on some US$20 billion (S$25.4 billion) of Canadian goods – things like wooden ice hockey sticks that are rarely used any more – are far from an economic game changer for the largest US trading partner after Mexico.
That represents just over 5 per cent of Canada’s exports to the US.
But the new tariffs mark an increase in tensions between US President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, and will likely make broader talks to renew the US-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement more difficult.
Carney said he had suspended trade negotiations and Canada would retaliate dollar for dollar on the new tariffs.
“I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the US and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa,” Carney said in a statement.
“They (negotiators) have worked hard, in good faith, to defend the interests of Canadians throughout these negotiations up until the very last minute.
“However, last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”
Carney, the only person to ever run the central banks of two major economies, was elected last year on promises to stand up to Trump, and remains broadly popular. Polls show most Canadians oppose making any concessions to Trump.
Hours earlier, the two sides had seemed close to an agreement that sources said would have lowered tariffs on steel, aluminium and cars and potentially brought American alcohol back to Canadian liquor stores.
“Tonight, Canada declined to finalise the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week,” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said during a White House briefing.
“This is a missed opportunity for Canada to partner with the United States, which is the fastest-growing economy in the G-7.”
A senior Trump administration official said the US offer would have put Canada in the best tariff position of any major exporter to the US, but that Canada had sought additional concessions, especially on steel, aluminium, cars and softwood lumber.
No additional talks are scheduled as the US implements the new duties, the official said.
Trump last month threatened to impose a raft of duties on a range of Canadian imports including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods and hockey equipment.
The tariffs, which do not qualify for preferential treatment under the US-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement, open up some already vulnerable sectors to potential severe damage that could lead to job losses and business closures, trade experts say.
The decision by the US administration followed three days of talks in Washington between Canada’s minister for trade with the US, Dominic LeBlanc, and Greer.
The new duties add to existing US tariffs on steel, lumber and cars which have taken major hits in the last 18 months, although the malaise has been largely contained in these sectors. REUTERS
